title: Insects and Spiders Detective Station
subtitle: Count legs and find clues
coreQuestion: How are insects and spiders different?
learningGoals: Know that insects usually have six legs.
Know that spiders are not insects and usually have eight legs.
Use observable clues to sort small animals.
misconceptions: All small creepy-crawly animals are insects.
Anything with wings must be an insect.

hero.title: Insects and Spiders Detective Station
hero.lead: Small animals can look similar, but a careful detective looks for clues.
hero.sceneExplanation: The main scene is a magnifying-glass observation table: butterflies, bees, ladybugs, ants, dragonflies, spiders, and centipedes hide among grass, stones, and flowers. When a child taps an animal, the page highlights leg count, antennae, and body sections.
hero.childPrompt: Tap a little animal. Count its legs and look for antennae.
hero.parentPrompt: The focus is evidence-based observation: do not judge only by flying or by whether it looks small and crawly.

classificationGroups.name: Insects
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Insects usually have six legs, antennae, and three main body parts.
classificationGroups.parentNote: For ages 5-8, focus on six legs + antennae + body sections.
classificationGroups.misconception: Not all insects fly; ants are insects too.

classificationGroups.name: Spiders
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Spiders usually have eight legs and no antennae.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Use spiders as a clear contrast with insects.
classificationGroups.misconception: A spider is not an insect.

classificationGroups.name: Other many-legged animals
classificationGroups.childExplanation: Some small animals have many legs, but that does not make them insects.
classificationGroups.parentNote: Centipedes are useful as a decoy category.
classificationGroups.misconception: Many legs does not mean insect.

representativeObjects.visualHint: eight legs, big eyes, no antennae
representativeObjects.commonMisread: Calling it an insect because it is small.

representativeObjects.name: Web spider
representativeObjects.childExplanation: This spider has eight legs and can make a web.

mechanism.title: How do we identify small animals?

steps.childExplanation: Six legs often points to an insect. Eight legs often points to a spider.
steps.parentNote: Counting legs is the most accessible first clue.

steps.childExplanation: Insects usually have antennae. Spiders do not.
steps.parentNote: Use simple visual labels or highlights.

steps.childExplanation: Insects have head, chest, and belly parts. Spiders look different.
steps.parentNote: No need for formal anatomical terms unless the child asks.

steps.shortTitle: Do not only look for wings
steps.childExplanation: Some insects fly, but some insects do not fly.
steps.parentNote: Ants help correct the ‘insects must fly’ misconception.

comparePairs.childConclusion: Counting legs is a good first clue.

comparePairs.title: Ant vs Spider
comparePairs.childConclusion: Both are small, but they are not the same kind.

comparePairs.title: Butterfly vs Centipede
comparePairs.childConclusion: Many legs does not mean insect.
